summary: Mazda's return to the mid-size car segment is a China-built electric liftback that Australian reviewers rate as quiet, well-finished and unusually polished for the money, with a $49,990 entry price that undercuts every Tesla Model 3 and the BYD Seal. The 77kWh usable LFP pack's 560km WLTP range and 195kW peak DC charging are competitive, but local testers consistently criticise the Europe-tuned suspension as too soft, the steering as too light off-centre, and the near-total reliance on a 14.6-inch touchscreen as a step backwards from Mazda's usual ergonomics. Both grades sit far below the $75,000 FBT exemption threshold, so the only real decision is interior trim.
pros: GT's $49,990 list price undercuts the cheapest Tesla Model 3 RWD by $4,910 and the entry BYD Seal by $3,000, while claiming 560km of WLTP range
195kW peak DC charging takes the LFP pack from 10-80 percent in around 24 minutes, well ahead of the 80kWh NMC version sold in continental Europe
High-voltage battery is covered for eight years or 160,000km, on top of the unconditional five-year, unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty
Rear-wheel drive with near-even 47/53 weight distribution, and Chasing Cars recorded 459km of real-world range over hilly terrain against the 560km claim
Rated to tow 1,500kg braked, where most electric sedans in this price band are limited to 1,000kg or are not rated to tow at all
cons: 337-litre boot to the parcel shelf is small for a mid-size liftback, against 682 litres in a Tesla Model 3
Almost everything except the windows, hazard lights and gear selector runs through the 14.6-inch touchscreen, including the wipers; reviewers report 30-45 minutes just to learn the menus
Australian reviewers rate the Europe-tuned damping too soft and the steering too light around straight ahead, and the mirror and indicator stalks are still laid out for left-hand drive
Brand-new nameplate with no Australian resale history, and Mazda's only previous EV here, the MX-30, sold in tiny numbers and depreciated heavily
